1408.title: Patience
1408.howItsDone: Christians count patience, called longsuffering in the King James Bible, among the fruit of the Spirit; churches teach it as something grown over a lifetime of prayer and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hope: Paul's riddle, hope that is seen is not hope. Your line was hope unseen.

A farmer has done everything a farmer can do. The field is plowed, the seed is in, the fence is mended. Now there's nothing left but the sky. He can't make it rain. He can't pull the shoots up to hurry them. He can only stand at the edge of the field in the evening and wait. The letter of James holds up that farmer as a picture, and yesterday Paul ended his riddle about hope with the same quiet word: we wait for it with patience.

Here's James, in the King James words: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain." Precious fruit. The farmer isn't bored. He's waiting for something he loves. In the Bible, patience isn't only putting up with things. It's a kind of love. Paul's chapter on love starts its list right here: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." Charity is the King James word for love, and the first thing it says love does is suffer long. Love waits. Then the Bible turns the same word toward God. When God passes before Moses on the mountain, he names himself: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." Longsuffering is part of God's own name in that passage. And a letter of Peter answers people asking why the Lord's promised coming seems slow, in surprisingly tender words: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish." If God seems slow, Peter says, it's because God is waiting for people. So patience here isn't a gritted jaw. It's the farmer at the fence, the parent at the door at midnight, the friend who lets you take your time. For Christians it's also the way God waits for them. Being patient with someone, in this picture, means loving them at their speed.

Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for right now, a person to change, an answer, a healing, a slow project, and notice where your body holds the waiting: a tight jaw, a restless hand. Breathe into that place, let it loosen a little, and ask what it would look like to wait for this the way the farmer waits, for something precious. If you pray, you can bring it to God in James's words, be patient therefore.
Patience. In the Bible, longsuffering: the farmer's wait for precious fruit, the first thing love does, and the way God himself waits.
Your line: love waits. Charity, the old word says, suffereth long. Rest well.

1409.title: The race (Hebrews 12:1–2)
1409.hook: run with endurance, looking to Jesus
1409.howItsDone: Some churches read Hebrews 12 at funerals and on All Saints' Day, remembering those who have gone before as a cloud of witnesses, and the image of the race appears in sermons, hymns and prayers for perseverance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, patience: the farmer waiting for precious fruit, and charity that suffereth long. Your line was love waits.

Late in a marathon. The crowd has thinned. The legs are lead. On this stretch the race stops being about speed and becomes about not stopping. Then someone on the curb shouts your name, and somehow you take the next step. An early Christian letter takes a scene like that, the long race and the crowd, and turns it into a picture of the life of faith. It doesn't promise a sprint. It promises a crowd.

Hebrews, chapter twelve, in the King James words: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us." Start with the cloud of witnesses. The chapter before is a long roll call: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab and more, people who trusted God without seeing the end. Now the writer gathers them around the runners like a cloud. Some readers picture them in the stands, watching; others hear witnesses as people whose lives bear witness. Either way, the runners aren't alone. Then, lay aside every weight. Nobody runs a long race in a winter coat. Some weights are sins. Some are just heavy: old grudges, worry, the need to look good. Then, run with patience. The Greek word here, hupomone, has more grit than the English: endurance, staying power, the strength to keep moving when it's hard. Yesterday's patience was a farmer waiting. Today's is a runner who won't quit. Then the turn: "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame." Eyes up. Not on your feet, not on the runner next to you. On the one who has already finished. Something waiting at the finish, the writer says, was worth the course.

Think of one long race you're in right now, a hard job, an illness, a marriage in a rough season, a habit you're trying to break, caring for someone, and notice one weight in it you could set down, even for today. Then picture your own cloud of witnesses in the stands: one or two people, living or gone, who ran something hard before you. If you pray, you can look to Jesus with the letter's words, the author and finisher of our faith.
The race. In Hebrews, the life of faith as a long run: a cloud of witnesses in the stands, every weight laid aside, and eyes on Jesus at the finish.
Your line: run with patience. Nobody on this track runs it alone. I'll be here tomorrow.

1410.title: Courage
1410.hook: courage is not having no fear, but acting while afraid (Joshua 1:9)
1410.howItsDone: Christians pray Joshua 1:9 and other verses of courage before surgery, exams, deployments and hard decisions, and churches tell the stories of Joshua, Esther and the saints and martyrs as examples of faith that acted while afraid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the race: a cloud of witnesses, every weight laid aside, eyes on Jesus. Your line was run with patience.

Moses is dead. The man who stood up to Pharaoh, who led the people through the sea, who spoke with God on the mountain, is gone. The job of leading the whole people across the Jordan falls on his assistant, Joshua. Right at the start of the book that carries his name, God speaks to Joshua, and what he says, more than once, isn't a battle plan. It's a sentence meant for someone who is frightened. Nobody tells a calm person not to be afraid.

Joshua chapter one, in the King James words: "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." Three things to notice. First, the command comes more than once in that chapter, the way you'd steady a friend at the edge of a high dive. Second, God doesn't tell Joshua the danger isn't real. The river still has to be crossed, the land still entered. Third, the reason. It isn't that Joshua is strong enough. It's the LORD thy God is with thee. The courage comes from company. So in this text, courage isn't the absence of fear. It's moving forward while afraid, because you aren't alone. Moses had said nearly the same words to Joshua before he died: be strong and of a good courage, he will not fail thee, neither forsake thee. Then there's Esther, queen of Persia, whose people are about to be destroyed. Her cousin Mordecai asks her to go to the king uninvited, which could cost her life: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Her answer doesn't sound brave at all: "and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." That's courage in Esther's story. Not a cheer. A frightened person deciding to go anyway, and asking her people to fast with her first.
screen: `BE STRONG AND OF A GOOD COURAGE.`
`THE LORD THY GOD IS WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been avoiding because you're afraid, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, an apology, a truth you need to tell, and name the fear plainly, with no need to pretend it away. If you pray, you can pray Joshua's verse, be strong and of a good courage, for the LORD thy God is with thee; if you don't, breathe with the fear for a minute and notice you're still here.
Courage. In Joshua and Esther, not the absence of fear, but going forward while afraid, because, the text says, God goes with them.
Your line: brave enough. Neither Joshua nor Esther had to be fearless first. Rest well.

1411.title: Making peace with your story
1411.hook: finding God even in the chapters you'd delete
1411.howItsDone: Christians bring the hard parts of their lives to God in prayer, confession, counseling and spiritual direction, and some practice a prayerful review of the day or of their life, looking for where God was present.

segments.voice: Yesterday, courage: Joshua and Esther, afraid and going anyway. Your line was brave enough.

If your life were a book, which chapter would you tear out? The thing you did, or the thing that was done to you. Some people carry a page like that, folded small. The Bible has a man with chapters he'd have every right to tear out: thrown in a pit by his brothers, sold as a slave, falsely accused, forgotten in prison. At the end of his story, he says something about those chapters to the very brothers who wrote them.

Joseph's jealous brothers strip off his coat, throw him in a pit, and sell him to traders bound for Egypt. There he's a slave, falsely accused, left in prison. Years later he runs Egypt's grain stores, and in a famine his brothers come to buy grain, not knowing him. There's a tearful reunion. But today's scene comes after their father Jacob dies. The brothers panic: now he'll pay us back. They send word asking forgiveness, and Joseph weeps. Then they fall down before him, and he says, in the King James words: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God? But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." Joseph doesn't call the pit good. He calls it evil, plainly. But he says God was at work in the same chapter, bending it toward saving lives. That's making peace with your story here: not pretending a hard chapter didn't happen, not tearing it out, but letting God hold it. The prophet Joel, after locusts strip the land, hears God promise: "I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten." And a psalm says even dark chapters aren't hidden: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." Christians explain how God works in suffering in different ways, and some are wary of easy answers. But in Genesis, even the pit is inside the story God is telling.
screen: `YE THOUGHT EVIL; GOD MEANT IT UNTO GOOD.`
`THE DARKNESS AND THE LIGHT ARE ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Choose one chapter you'd rather delete, not the worst if that's too much today, and see it plainly, the way Joseph named evil as evil. Then gently ask whether anything grew after it, knowing you don't have to find one; if you pray, bring it to God with Joel's line, I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten. If a hard chapter is still happening and you're not safe, please reach local emergency help, or in the US call or text 988.

1412.title: Thanks in all things (1 Thessalonians 5:18)
1412.hook: not for everything, but in everything
1412.howItsDone: Christians give thanks in prayers at meals, at bedtime and in church services, and a Christian funeral may give thanks for a life even while people grieve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph naming the evil, and God at work in the same chapter. Your line was every chapter held.

A hospital waiting room in the middle of the night. Bad coffee, a television nobody watches, a phone almost dead. On the table, someone has left a card with a sunrise on it: give thanks in all things. It can land like a slap. Thanks for this? For the scan, the layoff, the empty chair? But the line is older than the card, from a letter Paul wrote to the church in Thessalonica, and read slowly, it doesn't say what the card seems to say. One small word carries it.
screen: `A CARD WITH A SUNRISE ON IT.`

segments.voice: Near the letter's end, Paul fires off short lines like notes on a fridge. In the King James words: "Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." In every thing. Not for every thing. Some readers put it this way: the hard thing is a room, and thanks is something said inside it. Nobody is asked to call the diagnosis a gift. The thanks is for what's still true in there: a nurse who brings a blanket, a friend who answers at midnight, the breath you're still taking. Another letter, Ephesians, speaks of "giving thanks always for all things." Christians read that in more than one way. Some hear trust that God can bring good even out of what hurts. Others hear thanks for every good gift, offered at all times. Scripture doesn't hand over one tidy rule; the two lines sit side by side. Then there's Job. In one day he hears that his animals, his servants and his children are gone. He tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Look at the order. The torn robe comes first. The grief isn't skipped to get to the blessing. Both happen on the same ground, the same day. That's the shape of in, not for. The tears stay, and somewhere in the room, one good thing gets named.
screen: `IN, NOT FOR: THANKS INSIDE THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that's hard right now, and let it be as heavy as it is. Still inside it, look for one true good, a person who stayed, a warm cup, a text that came at the right time, and hold it; you don't need to be grateful for the hard thing itself. If you pray, thank God for that good in your own words; if not, let a quiet thank you rest on it.
Thanks in all things. Paul's line to the Thessalonians: in every thing give thanks. Thanks said inside the hard moment, without calling the hard moment good.
Your line: in, not for. One small word makes all the difference. See you tomorrow.

1413.title: Joy in hard times (Acts 5:41)
1413.hook: the apostles rejoiced to be counted worthy
1413.howItsDone: Christians remember the apostles' joy in Acts when they speak about faith under pressure, and churches pray for Christians in places where faith is costly; in hymns and sermons, joy is spoken of as something deeper than a good mood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thanks in all things: thanks said inside the hard room, not for it. Your line was in, not for.

The apostles have already been arrested once in this chapter of Acts. The story says an angel opened the prison doors in the night, and by morning they were back in the temple, teaching what they'd been told to stop. Now they stand before the council in Jerusalem, and Peter and the other apostles answer: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Tempers rise. Then Gamaliel, a teacher of the law and a Pharisee honored by the people, counsels patience: leave these men alone; if this is only human it will fall apart, and if it's from God, nobody will stop it. The council listens to him. Partly.

The council calls the apostles back in, has them beaten, orders them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and lets them go. Then the line that gives today its name, in the King James words: "And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name." Rejoicing. Not because the beating didn't hurt, or because they liked it. Look at what they rejoiced about: that they were counted worthy. A public beating was meant to shame them, to say these men are nobodies. They walked out reading it the other way around: being shamed for that name was an honor, a sign that they belonged to Jesus. Some readers hear them living out what Jesus said in the Sermon on the Mount, that if his followers were reviled for his sake, they should "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven." And the next verse says that daily, in the temple and in every house, they kept teaching. So the joy here isn't about feeling fine. It sits underneath the bruises, rooted in who they belong to. Nobody in the story goes looking for pain, and the story gives no reason to seek it out. But when the hard day came, they found something in it the hard day couldn't take.

Let today or this week come to mind as it really is, the tired parts included, then ask not what's going well but what you belong to: a family, a friendship, a faith, a piece of work you care about. Pick one and let a small gladness sit beside the tiredness; you don't need to feel happy. If you pray, you can thank God for what you belong to; if you don't, let the gladness be enough.
Joy in hard times. The apostles left the council beaten and rejoicing, counted worthy to suffer shame for his name: joy rooted in belonging, not in how the day went.
Your line: joy anyway. The bruises were real, and so was the gladness. Until tomorrow.

1414.hook: beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, and still going
1414.howItsDone: Christians read Paul's hardship list in 2 Corinthians as a picture of faith that keeps going, and some turn to it in a long, hard season of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, joy in hard times: the apostles left the council rejoicing, counted worthy to suffer shame. Your line was joy anyway.

A résumé is a list of wins. Degrees, titles, the big project you led. Nobody puts was fired twice at the top. In his second letter to the church in Corinth, Paul is under pressure to produce a résumé. Rival teachers have impressed some in the church, and Paul says he is "not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles." Some readers hear a dry smile in that phrase. So he agrees to boast, warning everyone first that he's speaking like a fool. Then he writes a very strange résumé.
screen: `A RÉSUMÉ IS A LIST OF WINS.`

segments.voice: Here's part of it, in the King James words: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep." He keeps going. Dangers on rivers, from robbers, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea. Then the ordinary misery of travel: "In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness." Read slowly, it stops sounding like a boast. It sounds like someone emptying his pockets. And after the stonings and shipwrecks comes the last item: "that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches." The final hardship isn't a wound. It's worry, lying awake over people he loves. He counts that too. Then he says why he wrote the list at all: "If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities." Infirmities means weaknesses. The next story he tells is almost funny. In Damascus the city was guarded to catch him, so he was let down through a window in the wall, in a basket. That's where the chapter ends: a grown man lowered in a basket. Some readers put it this way: the point isn't that Paul was tough. It's that he was still there. Beaten, cold, worried, smuggled out of a city, and still writing to the people he loved, still going.

Quietly start your own strange résumé: not the wins, but the things you got through, a loss, an illness, a move you didn't want, a year that went wrong, and the worry that kept you up counts too, as it did for Paul. Touch each one lightly, like counting on your fingers, without reliving it, and notice that you're here, on the other side of every one so far. If you pray, you can hand the list to God.
Paul's list. Beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, worried, and still going. It closes a week that walked through patience, the race, courage, your own story, thanks, and joy in hard times.
Your line: still here. In Paul's list, weakness is nothing to hide. That's today, done.

fork.reveal: he's lowered through a window in the wall, in a basket, and escapes. it's how this part of his boast ends: not a victory, a basket.

original.note: Greek: weakness. the King James calls it infirmities in 2 Corinthians 11:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of Paul's sufferings to show how tough he was.
what it means: Paul turns a boast upside down. instead of wins, he lists what he got through, worry included.
what a scholar hears: the list sits inside what Paul calls speaking as a fool, an answer to rivals in Corinth, and this part of it ends with an escape in a basket.
recall: a talk opening up the scripture just read
guess: a boast made of hardships and weaknesses, not of wins

the rules Paul set for anyone leading a church

chat.says: Why would Paul brag about being shipwrecked and beaten? Isn't that weird?
options: He boasts in his weaknesses on purpose; the point is he's still going, not that he's tough.
He wanted to prove he was stronger and tougher than every other apostle in the church.
He listed them to warn the Corinthians never to travel anywhere by sea.
chat.meaning: In 2 Corinthians 11:30 Paul says, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities. His list ends with worry, and then a basket.

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city whose church received Paul's letters

chiefest apostles.meaning: Paul's phrase for the rivals who impressed some in Corinth

Damascus.meaning: the city Paul escaped by being lowered in a basket
